name: controlled text input
desc: State holds the text, value displays it, onChange writes it back. Removing either half breaks the loop.

name: email input
desc: An email field is a text field with type email. The browser checks the shape on submit, and your own check still runs.

name: number input
desc: The value is a string even with type number. Keep the string in state and convert once, at submit.

name: select
desc: The value lives on select, not on option. A first option with an empty value works as the placeholder.

name: checkbox
desc: A single checkbox holds a boolean in checked. It does not use value, and it reads event.target.checked.

name: radio group
syntax: <input type="radio" name="room_type" value={type} checked={roomType === type} onChange={handle} />
desc: One state value for the group. Shared name, checked compared to that value, onChange stores the picked value.
body:
The shared `name` is what makes the browser treat the inputs as one group. Without it, clicking a second radio leaves the first one selected.

Radio choices drawn as cards keep the real input and hide it with CSS on the input, or use `appearance: none` plus a styled label. Replacing the input with clickable divs loses arrow key navigation and the group announcement for screen readers.

One value is pre-selected in the example. If the task wants no default, start the state as `''` and compare against that.

name: textarea
desc: The value is an attribute, not child text. Children would become initial content and React warns.
body:
In plain HTML the text sits between the tags. In JSX that reads as default content, so a controlled textarea must use `value` and `onChange` like every other text field.

`rows` sets the visible height, `maxLength` caps the input, and CSS `resize: vertical` stops a user from dragging the box wider than the layout.

name: one state object
desc: One object holds every field and one handler writes by name. Cheaper than one useState per field once a form grows.

name: submit handler
desc: Attach to form onSubmit and preventDefault first. Without it the browser reloads and state is lost.
body:
`onSubmit` on the form catches both the button click and the Enter key inside a text field. A click handler on the button catches only the click.

Validate before the request, and return early when the errors object is not empty. Disable the button while the request runs (`disabled={saving}`) so a second click does not post the same booking twice.

Read any `event.target.value` before the first `await`; after the request the DOM node may be gone even though the event object still exists.

name: validate function
syntax: function validate(form) { const errors = {}; return errors; }
desc: A pure function from values to an errors object. Empty object means valid.
body:
Keeping validation outside the component makes it testable without rendering and keeps the submit handler short.

Three moments to run it: on submit always, on blur when a field is left, on change only after the first failed submit. The last one avoids shouting at someone who is halfway through typing.

Error text should say what to do. "Phone needs at least 7 digits" is useful; "Invalid input" is not. Validate for the user, then validate again on the server, because the browser and your state are both outside the database.

name: field errors
desc: One errors object keyed by field name. Render each message under its field and mark the input invalid.
body:
`aria-invalid` tells assistive technology the field is wrong, and `aria-describedby` makes the message part of the field announcement. Without both, a screen reader user hears the label and the value but not the reason.

After a failed submit, move focus to the first invalid field. With a ref on the form this is a single query:

```jsx
const first = Object.keys(errors)[0];
formRef.current?.querySelector(`[name="${first}"]`)?.focus();
```

For long forms, an error summary at the top with the count of problems helps, but the per-field text is what people actually read.

name: reset a form
desc: A controlled form clears through state. form.reset() only restores DOM defaults and the state value returns.
body:
A `<button type="reset">` and `form.reset()` send the form back to its HTML default values. For a controlled input the next render puts the state value straight back, so the field looks like it refused to clear.

Uncontrolled inputs do reset with `form.reset()`. A file input is always uncontrolled and needs the ref line above.

A third option is a changing `key` on the form. React throws the subtree away and rebuilds it empty, which is handy when the form is generated from a record and the user switches records.

name: file input
desc: Always uncontrolled. Read event.target.files, send FormData, and clear it through a ref.
body:
React cannot set the value of a file input, so there is no controlled version. `files` is a read only `FileList`; take one entry, or use `Array.from(files)` when the input has `multiple`.

`accept="image/*"` only filters the picker. Check the type and the size in code before uploading, because a user can choose any file through the system dialog.

Send the file with `FormData` and let the browser set the multipart boundary. Do not put a `File` into `JSON.stringify`; it becomes `{}` and the upload arrives empty.

name: event.preventDefault()
desc: Stops the browser from submitting the form as a page navigation, which would reload and drop React state.
body:
A form without a handler submits to its `action` with a GET request, reloading the page. In a single page app that resets every piece of state and looks like a bug in the reset logic.

Call it before validation and before any `await`. The first line of the handler is the right place, so nobody adds a `return` above it later.

A button inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`. A button that only clears fields needs `type="button"`, or it will submit the form and fire `preventDefault` on the wrong path.
